\chapter{Ten Shapes, and Two That Lie}
\label{ch:bn-digits}
\hlchaptermodality{39}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read any number written in Bengali digits off a page -- a price, a year, a house number -- and I know exactly which two of the ten shapes my own reading will get wrong.}

Complete BN-R28-read-a-number: read a price off a shirt tag, read a year, and read a page number made of all four difficult shapes without hesitating.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[digit zero]{\bn{০} — the Bengali zero}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-zero}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{fourth} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{they} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{কালো}} off the page — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Sixty script lessons have taught you letters. Reading \textbf{\bn{কালো}} is reading letters. Every one of the twelve lessons ahead of you puts something on the page that is \textbf{not a letter at all}, and this book has never done that before.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{০}
\end{quote}

That is the Bengali digit \textbf{zero}.

Put it beside the zero you already read: \textbf{0}. A ring, closed, standing on the line, meaning \emph{none}. Bengali writes it the same way, and means the same thing.

That is not a coincidence and it is worth knowing before the other nine arrive. Wikipedia describes the Bengali numerals as \textbf{a variety of the Hindu–Arabic numeral system} — the same system as the digits on your keyboard, not a rival one. They are positional, they are read left to right, and \textbf{\bn{০}} does the same job at the end of a number as \textbf{0} does at the end of \textbf{10}.

There is no Bengali WORD for zero in this book yet. Today it is a shape you can read.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{০}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the five numbers you can already count — \emph{ek, dui, tin, chār, pā̃ch}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\bn{০}}? (\textbf{Zero}.) Is it a letter? (\textbf{No} — the first thing in this book that is not.) Which system do the Bengali digits belong to? (\textbf{The same one as 0–9}.)

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}; \href{https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengali\%E2\%80\%93Assamese\_numerals}{Wikipedia: Bengali–Assamese numerals}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[digit two]{\bn{২} — the Bengali two}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-two}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{০}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{first} — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{our} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{সাদা}} off the page — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{২}
\end{quote}

That is the Bengali digit \textbf{two}, and you can say it: \textbf{\bn{দুই}}.

Set it beside \textbf{2}. The top curls the other way and the foot is a diagonal rather than a bar, but the gross shape is the same — a turn at the top, a stroke running down to the right. Nobody would call \textbf{\bn{২}} a \emph{two} from nothing; anybody who already reads \textbf{2} can be told once and keep it.

So the count of shapes that cost you almost nothing now stands at two, and both of them mean \textbf{exactly what the shape you already know means}. Remember that. It stops being true in this chapter, and the place where it stops is the whole point of the chapter.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{২}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\bn{দুই}}, then read \textbf{\bn{২}} and \textbf{\bn{২০}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\bn{২}}? (\textbf{Two} — \textbf{\bn{দুই}}.) What is \textbf{\bn{২০}}? (\textbf{Twenty}.) How many shapes so far have meant the same as the shape you already knew? (\textbf{Both of them.})

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[digit three]{\bn{৩} — the Bengali three}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-three}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{২}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\bn{ঞ}} and say where it is made — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write the long \textbf{\bn{ী}} sign — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\bn{ী}} hangs on a letter and cannot stand alone. A digit is the opposite: it stands alone and hangs on nothing. Keep that difference in front of you, because this one looks like a letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{৩}
\end{quote}

That is the Bengali digit \textbf{three}, and you can say it: \textbf{\bn{তিন}}.

Now put it beside a letter you have had since the opening chapters:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{shape} \\
\midrule
the digit three & \textbf{\bn{৩}} \\
the letter \emph{o} & \textbf{\bn{ও}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

They are the same rounded body. \textbf{\bn{ও}} carries a stroke down its right-hand side; \textbf{\bn{৩}} does not, and that is the entire difference between a number and a letter here.

This is the only digit in the chapter that collides with a Bengali letter you have been taught, and the fix is one stroke wide: \textbf{if it has the tail on the right, it is a letter.}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{৩}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\bn{তিন}}, then read \textbf{\bn{৩}}, then read \textbf{\bn{ও}}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{৩০} and \bn{২৩}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What tells \textbf{\bn{ও}} from \textbf{\bn{৩}}? (\textbf{The stroke on the right.}) What is \textbf{\bn{২৩}}? (\textbf{Twenty-three.})

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[digit one]{\bn{১} — the Bengali one}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-one}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{৩}}, and say what tells it from \textbf{\bn{ও}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{fifth}, and the cardinal hiding inside it — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} put \textbf{-\bn{কে}} on a pronoun — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{নীল}} off the page — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{১}
\end{quote}

That is the Bengali digit \textbf{one}, and you can say it: \textbf{\bn{এক}}.

Nothing helps you here. \textbf{1} is a bare stroke; \textbf{\bn{১}} is a curl that starts high, comes down and hooks back to the right at the foot. There is no shape you already own to hang it on, and no letter it can be confused with.

That is worth naming rather than hiding: \textbf{\bn{০}}, \textbf{\bn{২}} and \textbf{\bn{৩}} each arrived carrying something. This one is simply learned, and so are the two after it.

Read \textbf{\bn{১০}} — one, then zero. \textbf{Ten.}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{১}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\bn{এক}}, then read \textbf{\bn{১}}, \textbf{\bn{১০}}, \textbf{\bn{১৩}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\bn{১}}? (\textbf{One} — \textbf{\bn{এক}}.) What did it bring with it that the first three digits did? (\textbf{Nothing.}) What is \textbf{\bn{১০}}? (\textbf{Ten.})

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[digit five]{\bn{৫} — the Bengali five}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-five}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{১}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{me}, the object form — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{তিন}} off the page — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

That last recall is the one this chapter exists for. \textbf{\bn{তিন}} is the \textbf{word} \emph{three}, spelled with three letters, and you have been able to read it for eighty lessons. \textbf{\bn{৩}} is the \textbf{digit} \emph{3}, and until two lessons ago you could not read it at all. A book can print either one, and they are not the same object.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{৫}
\end{quote}

That is the Bengali digit \textbf{five}, and you can say it: \textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}}.

Another one that brings nothing: a hooked stroke over an open bowl, like a \textbf{C} with a lid. \textbf{5} will not help you and no Bengali letter you know is close to it.

You can now read every number written out of \textbf{\bn{০} \bn{১} \bn{২} \bn{৩} \bn{৫}}, which is most of a page number and all of a small count.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{৫}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}}, then read \textbf{\bn{৫}}, \textbf{\bn{৫০}}, \textbf{\bn{১৫}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of these is a word and which is a digit — \textbf{\bn{তিন}}, \textbf{\bn{৩}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\bn{৫}}? (\textbf{Five} — \textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}}.) What is the difference between \textbf{\bn{তিন}} and \textbf{\bn{৩}}? (\textbf{One is the word, the other is the digit.})

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[digit six]{\bn{৬} — the Bengali six}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-six}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{৫}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{you}, as the one it happens to — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{এক}} off the page — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{৬}
\end{quote}

That is the Bengali digit \textbf{six}: a bowl at the foot with a tail rising away to the right. \textbf{6} does not help — its loop is at the bottom left and its stem comes down from above, which is nearly the reverse.

\textbf{And here your count runs out.} This book has taught you \textbf{\bn{এক}} to \textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}} and no further, so you can now read a number you have no Bengali word for. That is a real gap and it is worth stating plainly rather than covering: \textbf{from here to the end of the chapter you are learning to READ four numbers you cannot yet SAY.} The words are a separate piece of work.

Reading is still worth having on its own. A page number, a price and a date are all read far more often than they are said aloud.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{৬}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the five numbers you CAN say, then stop where the book stops
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\bn{৬}}? (\textbf{Six}.) Can you say it in Bengali yet? (\textbf{No} — the count in this book stops at \textbf{\bn{পাঁচ}}.) Does that stop you reading it? (\textbf{No.})

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[digit eight]{\bn{৮} — the Bengali eight}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-eight}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{৬}} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{who?} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say and read \textbf{\bn{কাপড়}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\bn{কাপড়}} is the first thing this book taught you that has a price on it. Hold on to it; you will read a price before this chapter ends.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{৮}
\end{quote}

That is the Bengali digit \textbf{eight}: an upright stroke with a single small bowl at the bottom right — much closer to a lower-case \textbf{b} than to anything numeric.

Look hard at it and notice what it is \textbf{not}. It has \textbf{one} bowl. \textbf{8} has \textbf{two}, stacked. Whatever the two-loop shape means in Bengali, it does not mean eight — and something has to mean it, because the shape exists.

That is the next lesson, and it is the one place in this chapter where the digits you already read will tell you a lie.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{৮}
  \item \emph{Say it:} how many bowls \textbf{\bn{৮}} has, and how many \textbf{8} has
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\bn{৮}}? (\textbf{Eight}.) How many bowls does it have? (\textbf{One.}) What does the two-bowl shape mean in Bengali? (\textbf{Not eight — and you are about to find out what.})

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[digit four]{\bn{৪} — the Bengali four}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-four}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{৮}}, and say how many bowls it has — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say and read \textbf{\bn{জামা}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{৪}
\end{quote}

That is the Bengali digit \textbf{four}, and you can say it: \textbf{\bn{চার}}.

It is two loops, stacked. It is the shape of an \textbf{8}.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape} & \textbf{in the digits you already read} & \textbf{in Bengali} \\
\midrule
two stacked loops & eight & \textbf{four} \\
upright with one bowl & \emph{nothing} & \textbf{eight} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the top row again. Every reflex you have says \emph{eight}, and it is wrong by four every single time — on a price, on a bus number, on a year.

The first three digits of this chapter arrived meaning exactly what their shape already meant to you. This one arrives meaning something else, and it is not a near miss: \textbf{\bn{৪}} and \textbf{8} are the same drawing.

The defence is the lesson before this one. If you are unsure, ask how many bowls: \textbf{two bowls is four; one bowl is eight.}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{৪}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\bn{চার}}, then read \textbf{\bn{৪}}, \textbf{\bn{৪৮}}, \textbf{\bn{৮৪}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\bn{৪}}? (\textbf{Four} — \textbf{\bn{চার}}.) What does your eye want it to be? (\textbf{Eight.}) Which question settles it? (\textbf{How many bowls?})

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A7\%AA}{Wiktionary: \bn{৪}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[digit nine]{\bn{৯} — the Bengali nine}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-nine}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{৪}}, and say what your eye wants it to be — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\bn{থ}} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{sari}, \emph{shāṛi} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{৯}
\end{quote}

That is the Bengali digit \textbf{nine}: a small closed body with a tail sweeping up and away to the right.

Once again, look at what it is \textbf{not}. \textbf{9} is a ring with a straight stem dropping below it. \textbf{\bn{৯}} has no dropped stem at all; its tail goes the other way, upward.

You have seen this pattern one lesson ago. The Bengali digit for eight did not take the \textbf{8} shape, and the \textbf{8} shape turned out to belong to four. The Bengali digit for nine does not take the \textbf{9} shape either — so ask the same question. \textbf{Something takes it.}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{৯}
  \item \emph{Say it:} which way the tail of \textbf{\bn{৯}} goes, and which way the stem of \textbf{9} goes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\bn{৯}}? (\textbf{Nine}.) Does it look like \textbf{9}? (\textbf{No} — the tail goes up, not down.) Which two Bengali digits have now refused the shape you expected? (\textbf{Eight and nine.})

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[digit seven]{\bn{৭} — the Bengali seven}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-seven}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{৯}}, and say which way its tail goes — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{here} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{glasses}, \emph{choshma} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\bn{৭}
\end{quote}

That is the Bengali digit \textbf{seven}, and it is the shape of a \textbf{9}: a closed body at the top with a straight stem dropping from its right side.

The chapter's second false friend, and the last shape in the set:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{shape} & \textbf{in the digits you already read} & \textbf{in Bengali} \\
\midrule
two stacked loops & eight & \textbf{four} \\
body with a dropped stem & nine & \textbf{seven} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both lies run the same way. In each case the Bengali digit \textbf{for} that value — \textbf{\bn{৮}} for eight, \textbf{\bn{৯}} for nine — took a different shape, leaving the familiar one standing empty; and in each case a smaller number moved into it.

Two out of ten shapes will actively mislead you. The other eight will not. That ratio is worth carrying, because it is the reason to slow down on exactly two shapes rather than to distrust the whole page.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \bn{৭}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the two shapes that lie, and what each one really means
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\bn{৭}}? (\textbf{Seven}.) What does the shape say? (\textbf{Nine.}) How many of the ten shapes mislead? (\textbf{Two.})

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[the two that lie]{The two that lie, and the eight that do not}

\label{lesson:BN-W07-digit-false-friends}



\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\bn{৭}}, and say what the shape claims — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{there} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
Ten shapes are in your hand. Here they are in order:

\begin{quote}
\bn{০} \bn{১} \bn{২} \bn{৩} \bn{৪} \bn{৫} \bn{৬} \bn{৭} \bn{৮} \bn{৯}
\end{quote}

A rule with an edge at each end, and both edges matter:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the band} & \textbf{what it means for you} \\
\midrule
where the shapes AGREE & \textbf{\bn{০}} is a \textbf{0} and means zero. \textbf{\bn{২}} is close to a \textbf{2} and means two. Trust these. \\
where they are simply NEW & \textbf{\bn{১} \bn{৩} \bn{৫} \bn{৬} \bn{৮} \bn{৯}} carry no Western digit's shape at all, so there is nothing to be misled by. \textbf{\bn{৩}} is the one to watch against a \textbf{letter}, not against a digit: \textbf{\bn{ও}} is the same body with a stroke down its right side. \\
where they LIE & \textbf{\bn{৪}} is drawn as an \textbf{8} and means \textbf{four}. \textbf{\bn{৭}} is drawn as a \textbf{9} and means \textbf{seven}. Nowhere else. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two of ten. Say them as a pair and they stay a pair: \textbf{the eight is a four, the nine is a seven} — and in both cases the Bengali digit that really means eight or nine is a shape you would never mistake for anything.

That is the whole rule. Eight shapes ask you to learn them; two ask you to un-learn something first.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the two that lie, then the eight that do not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two shapes mislead? (\textbf{The 8-shape, which is four; the 9-shape, which is seven.}) Which digit is confusable with a \textbf{letter} rather than with a digit? (\textbf{\bn{৩}}, against \textbf{\bn{ও}}.) How many of the ten are safe? (\textbf{Eight.})

Sources: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0980.pdf}{Unicode Bengali chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Reading a number off a page}

\label{lesson:BN-R28-read-a-number}



\begin{quote}
Two recalls, then the reading.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} name the two shapes that lie — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{where?} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Nothing new arrives here.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\bn{কাপড়}}, then read a price beside it — \textbf{\bn{৮০}}
  \item \textbf{\bn{কোথায়}?}, then read a house number — \textbf{\bn{৩৪}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
Sixty script lessons taught you letters, and one of them, long ago, taught you to read \textbf{\bn{তিন}}. That was the \emph{word}. Until this chapter you could not read \textbf{\bn{৩}}, and so you could not read a price, a date, a clock face or a page number — the things a reader meets far more often than they meet a sentence.

Ten shapes closed that. Eight of them were simply learned; \textbf{\bn{০}} and \textbf{\bn{২}} cost almost nothing because the Bengali digits and the digits on your keyboard are one system rather than two; and two of them — \textbf{\bn{৪}} and \textbf{\bn{৭}} — had to be taken away from a reflex before they could be given to you.

What this chapter did \textbf{not} do is teach you to SAY six, seven, eight, nine or zero. Those words are not in this book yet. You can read every number on the page and speak the first five of them, and the gap between those two abilities is now the most useful thing left undone in this column.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\bn{৪৭}}. (\textbf{Forty-seven} — not ninety-eight.) Which numbers can you now read? (\textbf{All of them.}) Which can you say? (\textbf{One to five.})
\end{tcolorbox}
